name: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100
description: The CIFAR-10 dataset has 6000 examples of each of 10 classes and the CIFAR-100 dataset has 600 examples of each of 100 non-overlapping classes. Both are labeled subsets of the 80 million tiny images dataset, consisting of 32x32 colour images collected from the web. CIFAR-10 classes include airplane, automobile, bird, cat, deer, dog, frog, horse, ship, and truck. CIFAR-100 contains 100 classes organized into 20 superclasses of five classes each.
creator: Alex Krizhevsky
citeAs: Alex Krizhevsky, 'Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images', April 8, 2009.
rai:dataCollection: Students were paid to label a subset of the 80 million tiny images dataset. Each labeler was given a class and asked to examine all images found with that class as the search term, as well as images found with hyponyms of the main search term (as defined by WordNet). Labelers were instructed to reject images that did not belong to their assigned class. The authors personally verified every label submitted by the labelers. Duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm using a rejection threshold liberal enough to capture not just perfect duplicates but also re-saved JPEGs.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data is the 80 million tiny images dataset collected by groups at MIT and NYU. They assembled it by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in the lexical database WordNet, using several search engines including Google, Flickr, and Altavista, keeping roughly the first 3000 results for each search term. Images were downscaled to 32x32 pixels. The dataset contains 80 million colour images spread across 79000 search terms.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The 80 million tiny images dataset was collected over the span of six months (exact dates not specified).
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: After collecting images for each search term, perfect duplicates and images in which an excessively large portion of the pixels were white were removed. For the labeled subset, duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm using a rejection threshold liberal enough to capture not just perfect duplicates but also re-saved JPEGs. The dataset was divided into a training set (5000 images per class) and a test set.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were downscaled to 32x32 pixels. ZCA whitening transformation was applied to decorrelate pixel values. The 1000 least significant directions of variance (principal components) were deleted from the dataset. For patch-based experiments, 32x32 images were divided into 25 8x8 patches plus a 26th globally subsampled 8x8 patch.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Each labeler was given a class and asked to examine all images found with that class as the search term and with hyponym search terms. Labelers were instructed to reject images not belonging to their assigned class based on criteria: (1) the class name should be high on the list of likely answers to 'What is in this picture?'; (2) the image should be photo-realistic (line drawings rejected); (3) the image should contain only one prominent instance of the object; (4) the object may be partially occluded or seen from an unusual viewpoint as long as its identity is clear. Labelers were paid a fixed sum per hour. The authors personally verified every label submitted.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The authors personally verified every label submitted by the labelers. False positives (incorrectly included images) were considered worse than false negatives (incorrectly excluded images).
rai:annotatorDemographics: Students (paid per hour spent labeling; no further demographic details provided).
rai:dataBiases: The search term used to find an image provides it with a rough label, although it is extremely unreliable due to the nature of online image search technology.
rai:dataLimitations: The original 80 million tiny images dataset has no reliable class labels, making it hard to use for object recognition experiments. The labeled subsets (CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100) were created to address this. All experiments were conducted with CIFAR-10 as CIFAR-100 was only very recently completed at the time of writing.
rai:dataUseCases: Training and testing of object recognition and classification models. Used for unsupervised training of deep generative models (RBMs and DBNs) and supervised classification experiments. CIFAR-100 classes can also be used as negative examples for CIFAR-10.
